newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany spruces up debt market for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany spruces up debt market for EMU.

text.p: Germany, ever mindful that the loss of the mark through European economic and monetary union (EMU) could hurt its financial centre, announced on Tuesday measures to attract international investors to its bond market.
A senior finance ministry official gave a strong indication Bonn will convert outstanding federal debt to euros from the planned start of the single currency in January, 1999.
The government also sold a 30-year bond for the first time in three years and launched bond stripping, which is the separate trading of registered interest and principal of securities.
The latter move brings Germany in line with the U.S., France, Belgium and the Netherlands where stripping is already established. Britain and Spain are expected to follow this year.

Juergen Stark, state secretary in the finance ministry, said he would propose to Finance Minister Theo Waigel that all tradable federal debt, which is about half the total federal debt of 900 billion marks ($515.5 billion), be converted to euros.
A decision would be taken at a cabinet meeting before the the summer break, Stark said.
Analysts said the move to euros was vital to ensure the German debt market, the world's third largest, held its preeminent role after the single currency's launch.

France has already said it will convert its outstanding debt to euros and if Germany does not follow suit, it will not have enough euro-denominated government debt to satisfy investors, who might opt for French bonds instead.
"It would be fatal if they didn't convert the debt," said Helmut Kaiser, bond market analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The sale of a 30-year government bond, bearing a 6.52-percent coupon, underscored Bonn's commitment to meeting investors' demands for debt across the full range of the maturity spectrum, Stark told a news conference held jointly with Bundesbank Deputy President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum.
"This is an important aspect against the backdrop of the third stage of monetary union when the mark disappears as a competitive advantage for the financial centre," Stark said.
The government sold three billion marks of the new 30-year bond on Tuesday as a first tranche and will auction a second portion on Wednesday.
That bond, together with a 30-year, 6.25 percent coupon bond maturing in 2024 and two 10-year bonds issued in 1997, will be strippable.
Stripping gives investors tax advantages and should make government debt issuance cheaper by making the bonds more attractive to investors.
It also closes gaps in the yield curve because coupons for every year from one to 30 years will be tradable. "Every point of the yield curve can be priced," Gaddum said.
Outstanding strippable bonds will initially be modest at about 77 billion marks, but Stark said Bonn would issue more strippable 10-year and 30-year debt.

The news conference marked a show of unity between Bonn and the Bundesbank, in stark contrast with their recent conflict over Bonn's abortive plan to seek a payout in 1997 from reserves held at the bank.
"The Bundesbank and the finance ministry want to make sure that German debt continues to be the benchmark in Europe," said Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
Kraemer said it was interesting to note a recent shift in the Bundesbank's attitude towards the more technical financial market products.
Tuesday's measures follow a series of steps to spruce up Germany's financial centre, most recently by freeing up securities repurchase business from the Bundesbank's minimum reserve requirement.
Also, the Bundesbank last year sanctioned the issuance of six-month Treasury discount paper, called Bubills, and of two-year Treasury notes.
